extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying introductory real analysis / calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory exposition of variables, functions, limits, continuity, sequences, monotone sequence principle, and related concepts for students learning calculus and elementary real analysis. Includes definitions, tests, examples, and typical pathologies (discontinuities, oscillation, divergence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and domain of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables denote objects chosen at will from a whole set S; e.g., X and Y with domain S express general laws such as X + Y = Y + X. The domain S need not be numbers and may be finite or infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: S could be integers, circles in the plane, closed polygons, population members, or the set {0,1,2,3,4} of remainders modulo 5. Use variables to state laws valid for all members of S; constants are particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous variable and its domain
rubrics_metrics.description: A numerical variable x is called continuous when its domain S is an interval a < x < b of the real axis (the domain may be extended to infinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical domains: entire real line, positive reals x>0, or any interval. Pairs of continuous variables (x,y) represent points in the plane when each ranges over a region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function definition (U = F(X))
rubrics_metrics.description: If with each value of a variable X there is associated a definite value of another variable U, then U is called a function of X, written U = F(X). X ranges over domain S and U ranges over range T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: perimeter mapping triangles to positive numbers; projective transformation mapping points of one plane S to points of another T. Different X may map to same U (not injective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When U = F(X), X is the independent variable (its values are chosen freely) and U is the dependent variable (its value depends on X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case: if U is same for all X (range T consists of one element), U is constant; treat constants as functions with single-element domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as mapping / biunique mapping (invertibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mapping is biunique (one-to-one correspondence) when F(X1) ≠ F(X2) whenever X1 ≠ X2; in that case an inverse function exists. For one-variable mappings, inverse functions exist for biunique maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: projective transformations of one line have form (ax+b)/(cx+d); inverse given analytically. For mappings between planes, inverse requires solving a system and biuniqueness of the transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of several variables and representations
rubrics_metrics.description: When two quantities x and y are independent, u = f(x,y) denotes a function of two variables; geometrically represented by a surface in 3D (x,y,u) or by contour (level) curves f(x,y)=c in the x,y-plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: u = sqrt(1 - x^2 - y^2) (spherical surface), u = ax + by + c (plane), u = xy (hyperbolic paraboloid). Level curves help visualize heights (values) in the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound (composed) functions
rubrics_metrics.description: New functions can be created by composing functions: if z = g(x) and u = h(z), then u = h(g(x)) is the compound function u = f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: u = sqrt(1 + x^2) as h(g(x)) with g(x)=1+x^2 and h(z)=sqrt(z); functions like sin(1/x) come from composition and may have restricted domains where inner function undefined (e.g., x = 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity (intuitive and pointwise test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly, a function is continuous if its graph is an uninterrupted curve. More precisely, f is continuous at x = x_i if f(x) approaches the value f(x_i) as x approaches x_i from either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test continuity at x_i, let x approach x_i from the right and left; if both one-sided limits exist, are equal, and equal f(x_i), the function is continuous at x_i. If this holds for every point in an interval, the function is continuous on that interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of discontinuities (removable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discontinuity is removable if redefining f(x_i) appropriately (or defining it where undefined) makes the function continuous at x_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: u = x/x is identically 1 for x ≠ 0; if we define u(0)=1 the function becomes continuous everywhere. Similarly, redefining a value to match the common limit removes the discontinuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of discontinuities (jump/discontinuous from sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discontinuity of the second type (jump) occurs when limits approached from the right and left at x_i exist but are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example illustrated by a function with f(0) = -1 but right-hand limit +1; left and right limits differ so continuity cannot be achieved by redefining the single point value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of discontinuities (essential / oscillatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: An essential discontinuity occurs when even one-sided limits do not exist (e.g., because function oscillates arbitrarily near the point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(x) = sin(1/x) near x=0 has infinitely many oscillations and no one-sided limit; such behavior cannot be cured by redefining the function at the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of discontinuities (infinite / unbounded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discontinuity where the function tends to infinity as x approaches x_i (no finite limiting value) is of the infinite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: u = 1/x near x=0; as x→0 from either side u→±∞. Such discontinuities are essential and cannot be removed by redefining f(x_i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–N definition of limit of a sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence {a_n} has limit a if, for every positive number ε (no matter how small), there exists an integer N (depending on ε) such that |a - a_n| < ε for all n > N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: terms eventually lie inside any chosen interval centered at a. Algorithmic description: given ε, find N so that from N onward all terms are within ε of a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent vs divergent sequences and 'tends to infinity'
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence with a limit is convergent; a sequence without a limit is divergent. If sequence terms eventually exceed any preassigned K, we say the sequence tends to infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,2,3,... tends to infinity; alternating or oscillating sequences may be divergent. Notation: lim a_n = ∞ denotes divergence to infinity (though ∞ is not a number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone sequence principle (monotone bounded convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any monotone increasing sequence that has an upper bound must converge to a limit (and similarly any monotone decreasing sequence with a lower bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: monotone and bounded sequences cannot 'escape' and must approach a limit; the proof can be given via decimal expansions, nested intervals, or Dedekind cuts. This principle is used to define limits and real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using monotone sequences to define operations / numbers (example e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some important numbers are defined as limits of monotone bounded sequences. Example: define a_n = 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + ... + 1/n! ; the sequence is monotone increasing and bounded (a_n < 3), so it converges — its limit is the number e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows methodology: construct monotone bounded sequences whose limits define constants (e, sqrt(2), etc.). The sequence's monotonicity and explicit upper bound give existence of limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical/level-curve test for functions of several variables (continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function u = f(x,y) is continuous at (x_i,y_i) if f(x,y) approaches f(x_i,y_i) when (x,y) approaches (x_i,y_i) from any direction or in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric view: continuity corresponds to the surface u=f(x,y) being unbroken; contour/level curves f(x,y)=c give 2D representations and help visualize continuity and level sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse function remark for multivariable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For functions of two variables u = f(x,y), a single relation u = f(x,y) does not in general allow solving for x and y as functions of u (inverse function becomes meaningless in general), except when considering the mapping viewpoint (transformations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transformation/mapping notion: a biunique and bicontinuous mapping in two dimensions is represented by two functions x' = f(x,y), y' = g(x,y) and may have an inverse mapping when biunique.
